title: Decimal Comparer
description: Compare decimals place by place from the whole number parts, see the first place that differs decide, and put decimals in ascending or descending order.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

zones.layout: board, key only: no question bar, only its key at the right end of the top row (the question is on the bubble); the working area is the whole card (64, 108, 1472 x 520) until the child taps Answer, when the answer drawer (as tall as the working area, the key on its top row reading Close) slides in from the right
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one small dot per phase at the footer's right (72-unit finger boxes, centred on the bubble), no text; in user AND AI mode each is a button (data-control phase-dot, data-phase k) that starts its phase

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Compare two decimals by their whole number parts and then place by place, and arrange decimals in ascending or descending order.
writeup.look: Two decimal cards with their points in one line over a place strip, bars to scale on a tape under them, and an ordering ladder on the last phase.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Decimal Comparer' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x sixty-four, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many places have been compared so far, counting from the left. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x sixty-four, y 202. The two cards stand at x 110, y 230 and y 320, each 520 wide and 76 tall, their large near-black points on one vertical line at x 330, the digits deep blue, over a place strip at y 410. A pair that matches fades to half strength; the first pair that differs lights amber, labelled Decides, and the sign is written green between the cards at x 680. The tape runs along y 500 from x 110 to x 1030, marked in ones and tenths, with one bar for each card drawn to scale above it. The Make like button sits at x 720, y 230; zeros it writes are violet, labelled Added zero. On the last phase the ordering ladder of four rungs fills the lower half from y 420, each rung 520 wide, with a slot for the sign between every pair and the Ascending and Descending switch at x 720, y 440. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a point key and the two sign keys, for setting a decimal or typing the greater decimal, a sign or an order into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. A decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it. The result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum, a difference or what is left, is green, with its shaded parts. Ten of one place traded for one of the next, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written after the point to line decimals up is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded part stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the decimal point is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label, Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left or Place holder, before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last ladder in order, each sign between its pair and the deciding places lit.

phases.does: taps Compare, watches the whole number parts light, and taps the greater card
phases.goal: when the whole number parts differ, the greater whole number part decides
phases.says: Look at the whole numbers first. Is it settled already?
phases.check: Away from the screen: can a decimal with a smaller whole number part ever be greater? Why not?
phases.feels: the comparison settling before the point is even reached
phases.hands: Write two decimals with different whole number parts on slips, one above the other with the points in one line. Cover everything after the points and say which is greater.
phases.tries: First rung: read the two whole number parts. Second rung: say which is greater. Third rung: the same task with one digit after each point.

writeup.delight: On the third phase, when the tenths decide, the bar of the longer decimal shrinks back beside the other with a soft slide, as if it had been caught standing on its toes.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with two decimal cards standing one above the other, their points in one line, and the bars drawn to scale on the tape under them. Nothing is lit. On the fourth phase the cards wait in a row above the empty ordering ladder instead. One thing moves, once: the Compare button, or the first card over the ladder, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two decimals compared place by place, with or without the Make like button, and any four on the ordering ladder. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on whole number parts, tenths and hundredths, more digits, and ordering.
voiceLines: Two decimals, their points in one line.
Look at the whole numbers first. Is it settled already?
The ones match. Which place is next?
Smallest first. Then flip it, greatest first.
Two new decimals. Look at the whole numbers first.
Free play. Compare any decimals, and order any four.
Start from the left. Which place is the first to differ?
The first place that differed decided every time.

observations.why: a whole one is more than any number of tenths and hundredths.
observations.soWhat: when the whole number parts differ, the greater whole number part decides.
observations.observe: When the whole numbers differed, nothing after the point was ever lit.

observations.why: every place further right is worth less than the one that differs.
observations.soWhat: the first place that differs decides.
observations.observe: Matching places faded, and the comparison stopped at the first pair that differed.

observations.why: more digits after the point only means smaller parts, not more of them.
observations.soWhat: more digits after the point does not make a decimal greater.
observations.observe: The longer decimal sometimes had the shorter bar.

observations.why: zeros at the end after the point change nothing.
observations.soWhat: writing zeros to make like decimals is a help, not a rule.
observations.observe: The comparison came out the same with or without the Make like zeros.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: Compare walks from the left: the whole number parts light amber and decide, the ribbons are laid to scale, the greater card is ringed and the sign is written.
Phase 2: Compare walks from the left: the matching ones fade, the first place after the point that differs lights amber, the ribbons are laid to scale and the sign is written.
Phase 3: Compare walks from the left and the tenths decide; the ribbons are laid to scale and the longer decimal's ribbon is seen to stop first; the sign is written.
Phase 4: Each pair's first differing place lights amber on the ladder, the lowest step is ringed, and the right order is written above the ladder.

voice.opening: Two decimals, their points in one line.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play: compare new pairs and put new rows of cards in order.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again
voice.onFinish: The first place that differed decided every time.
voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3, 4: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

question.en: Tap the card that is greater, 15.2 or 8.96.
Now 19.8 or 21.05: tap the greater one.
Last pair, 30.001 or 29.999: which card is greater?

items.planAnswer: 30.001, because 30 > 29. The digits after the point do not matter

question.en: Next, 4.51 or 4.53: which one is more?

items.planAnswer: 4.53. The ones and the tenths match, and 3 hundredths is more than 1 hundredth

items.planQuestion: One ribbon is 2.64 m long and another is 2.6 m long. Which is longer?

question.en: One ribbon is 2.64 m and one is 2.6 m long: tap the longer one.

items.planAnswer: The 2.64 m ribbon. The ones and the tenths match, and 4 hundredths is more than 0 hundredths

question.en: Tap the card that is greater, 0.7 or 0.625.
Now 0.79 or 0.8: pick the greater one.

items.planAnswer: 0.8, because 8 tenths is more than 7 tenths

question.en: Last pair, 0.587 or 0.6: which one is more?

items.planAnswer: 0.6, because 6 tenths is more than 5 tenths

question.en: Put 3.09, 3.9 and 3.009 in descending order, greatest first.
This time, 5.06, 5.6 and 0.56 in ascending order, smallest first.
Four cards now, 12.4, 1.24, 12.04 and 124: greatest first.

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

getState: toolId, mediaId, mode, mountPhase, phase, phases, conceptId, objectiveIds, step, steps, item, items, stage (teach, demo, ask, win, idle, summary, free), question, questionText, choices, typed, keypadOpen, tries, answered, firstTry, score, maxScore, answerShown (only after the answer), complete, questionCount, muted (the sound effects), speaking (always false: the lesson is silent), voice ("silent"), mascot, summaryRow, played, classroom, held (a classroom's parked piece of a long line), instruction (the pinned line), hint (the hint under it, or null), guideStep / guideSteps / guideOn (a guide-steps phase only), compared, decides, null, measured, picked, null, complete

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files, on in every mode (the sound button switches them): correct, wrong (soft), win at a phase end, cheer at the last, a tick when a piece snaps, and cut, settle and trade where the picture moves
